needs_redesign.capability: Settings Watch section — connection status, feature configuration, and data telemetry
needs_redesign.why: Status and telemetry port to WatchConnectivity, but the mental model changes. `WCSession` gives `isPaired`, `isWatchAppInstalled`, `activationState`, and `isReachable` directly — no capability query, no node enumeration, and no need for Android's careful distinction between CapabilityClient (which proves the app is installed) and NodeClient (which does not). The 15s discovery timeout, the nearby-node preference, and the fallback logic all become unnecessary. What does not port is the watch-face gallery and the watch-app APK push, which are listed as impossible; and the feature toggles change meaning, because with no custom face they now configure the watch app's own screens and its WidgetKit complications rather than a face.
options: Keep the toggles but retarget them at the watch app UI and its accessory widgets, dropping the ones that only make sense on a face.
Drop the configuration card entirely and let each widget be configured through WidgetKit's own intent-based configuration UI on the watch.
Both: app-level toggles synced from the phone, plus per-widget configuration for placement-specific choices.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, with the toggle set trimmed honestly: keep Show IoB, Show Glucose Graph, Alert Vibration, Graph Range (1H/3H/6H, coerced to a valid value with a fallback of 3), Theme, and the graph overlay toggles (basal area, bolus markers, IoB overlay, activity-mode bands) as configuration for the watch app's main screen and its `accessoryRectangular` widget. Drop "Show Seconds", which has no meaning without a face. Sync via `WCSession.updateApplicationContext` (latest-value-wins, exactly the right semantics for config) and keep the Android rule that the sync reads `aiTtsEnabled`/`aiTtsVoice` from the canonical store rather than the config copy, so a value set on the chat screen is never overwritten. Keep the telemetry card verbatim, including the 20–500 mg/dL validation of the reported value, the explicit "(wire, mg/dL)" label so a canonical wire value is never misread as a display value, the `formatTimeAgo` thresholds, and the "Could not read watch data" failure state. Keep the two hint cards for the not-installed and not-reachable states, retargeted at TestFlight installation guidance.

needs_redesign.capability: Settings About — version info, licenses entry, and update awareness
needs_redesign.why: The version rows and the Open Source Licenses entry port unchanged. The in-app update state machine cannot: downloading and installing an app build is impossible on iOS (listed separately). The capability that remains is telling the user a newer build exists and getting them to it.
options: Drop update checking entirely and rely on TestFlight's own update notifications.

Keep a version check against the GitHub Releases API and, when a newer build is available, show the version, release notes, and a button that opens TestFlight (`itms-beta://` or the public beta link) or the App Store.
Show only the installed version and build number with no remote check.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2, with the state machine collapsed to Idle → Checking → (UpToDate | Available | Error). Reuse the existing GitHub error copy (403 rate limit, 404 no dev release, other status codes) and the channel selection between the stable release and the dev tag. Everything after 'Available' is replaced by a single 'Open TestFlight' action. The standalone HTTP client with no auth or base-URL interception ports as a separate `URLSession`; the https-only enforcement and the github.com / objects.githubusercontent.com host allowlist remain good practice for the metadata request even though nothing is downloaded. Keep the version, build type, and active-driver protocol rows, and keep the Open Source Licenses row exactly where it is.

needs_redesign.capability: Settings Battery Optimization card — the background-monitoring-reliability advisory
needs_redesign.why: iOS has no per-app battery optimization exemption, no `isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations` equivalent, and no Settings destination for such a control — that specific request is not available on the platform. But the card's actual purpose (warn the user when a device setting will kill overnight monitoring, and send them to the fix) has real iOS analogues, and they are arguably more important here because Core Bluetooth background delivery and any background refresh are what keep monitoring alive.
options: Report `UIApplication.shared.backgroundRefreshStatus` (available / denied / restricted) and deep-link to Settings when it is not available.
Report `ProcessInfo.processInfo.isLowPowerModeEnabled` and explain that Low Power Mode reduces background activity and can delay alerts.

Report Bluetooth authorization and power state via `CBCentralManager` and, if the app relies on state restoration, warn when the user has force-quit the app (which permanently suspends Core Bluetooth restoration until relaunch).
Show nothing and rely on the honest 'NOT watching' surfaces elsewhere.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Options 1, 2, and 3 together in one card that renders only when a pump is paired and at least one condition is degraded, keeping the Android placement between Plugins and Sync and its red warning treatment. The force-quit condition (option 3) is the closest true analogue of Android's battery-optimization kill: on iOS a user swiping the app away from the app switcher stops Core Bluetooth state restoration from relaunching it, which is exactly the 'Android may stop the pump connection when the screen is off' failure in iOS clothing, and it deserves explicit copy. Re-evaluate on every foreground transition, as the Android card does on every `loadState()`.

impossible.capability: Runtime/custom plugin installation and removal — the "Custom Plugins" card, Add Plugin from a user-supplied .jar, per-plugin Remove that deletes its settings, and the untrusted-source warning
impossible.why: iOS forbids downloading and executing code that is not part of the signed app bundle. App Review Guideline 2.5.2 prohibits apps that download, install, or execute code which introduces or changes features or functionality, and there is no supported dynamic-loading mechanism for third-party binaries on iOS. This is already settled by the project's decision that drivers are compile-time-linked Swift modules; the Settings surface has to reflect that.
impossible.closest_alternative: A built-in driver registry: every supported pump driver ships inside the app, is listed with its name and version, and can be enabled or disabled (keeping the deactivation confirmation dialog, since deactivating a driver can stop glucose monitoring). Community drivers are contributed as pull requests and arrive in the next TestFlight build. If a 'this driver is community-maintained and not verified' provenance signal is wanted, ship it as per-driver metadata on the card rather than an install-time warning.

impossible.capability: In-app self-update — checking GitHub Releases, downloading an app build, verifying its size, and launching an installer
impossible.why: There is no way for an iOS app to install another iOS app or replace itself. Guideline 2.5.2 forbids downloading executable code, and there is no installer intent, no FileProvider-style install handoff, and no user-approved sideload path from inside an app on stock iOS.
impossible.closest_alternative: TestFlight is the update channel: it notifies testers, and builds install through the TestFlight app. The app may still call the GitHub Releases API to detect that a newer build exists and show the version, size, and release notes, but the only action available is a button that opens TestFlight or the App Store. Keep the https-only and host-allowlist rules for the metadata request even though nothing is downloaded.

impossible.capability: Pushing a watch app build to the paired watch — the Watch App Update card's download → push → install state machine, its 100 MB download cap, and its install timer
impossible.why: watchOS apps are distributed only as part of the paired iPhone app's bundle, installed by the system through the App Store or TestFlight. No API installs, sideloads, or transfers an app to the watch, and the same code-download prohibition applies.
impossible.closest_alternative: Report the installed watch app version (obtained over WatchConnectivity) alongside the phone version, flag a mismatch as a diagnostic, and instruct the user to update the iPhone app from TestFlight — the watch app follows automatically once the Watch app's 'Automatic App Install' is on, or manually from the Watch app's install list.

impossible.capability: Custom watch faces — the watch-face gallery (Digital Full / Analog Mechanical variants), pushing a face to the watch, and face-level configuration such as showing seconds
impossible.why: watchOS does not permit third-party watch faces. No API renders a face, and no app can install a face of its own design. This is the single largest genuine feature loss in the port and should be stated plainly in the PRD rather than described as a redesign.
impossible.closest_alternative: Three partial substitutes, none of which is a face: (1) WidgetKit accessory complications (accessoryCircular, accessoryCorner, accessoryInline, and accessoryRectangular, which can show a small glucose graph) that the user places on any Apple face — this recovers glanceability and the chat/BG tap targets, including the Android chat complication, via `widgetURL` deep links; (2) Smart Stack widgets on watchOS 10+, which surface BG/IoB with relevance-based presentation without any face configuration; (3) optionally, bundling `.watchface` sharing files that pre-configure an Apple face (e.g. Modular Ultra or Infograph) with the app's complications and an accent color, which the user installs with one tap — this gives a curated 'Digital' and 'Analog' starting point built from Apple's face types, but the rendering, layout, and overlays are Apple's, not the app's. The graph overlays (basal area, bolus markers, IoB overlay, activity-mode bands) survive only inside the watch app's own screens and the accessoryRectangular widget.

impossible.capability: Choosing an arbitrary system ringtone or notification sound for an alert category (RingtoneManager picker, arbitrary content URIs, persistable read URI permission, per-URI title resolution)
impossible.why: iOS exposes no API to enumerate, preview, or select the system ringtone/alert-sound library, and notification sounds can only reference files inside the app bundle or the app container's Library/Sounds directory (Linear PCM, MA4, µLaw, or aLaw packaged as .aiff/.wav/.caf, 30 seconds maximum). There is no cross-app URI permission model, so the persistable-read-permission behavior has no counterpart.
impossible.closest_alternative: Ship a curated set of sounds inside the app — a deliberately aggressive alarm set for low alerts, a notification set for high alerts and AI — plus an explicit Silent option for AI, with in-app preview playback so the picker still feels like a choice. Optionally allow the user to import an audio file into the app container, which is the only way to support a user-supplied sound.

impossible.capability: The notification channel model — per-category sound, importance, vibration pattern, and DND-bypass settings that the user can independently tune in system settings, plus channel deletion/recreation to change a sound
impossible.why: iOS has no notification channels. The system offers only app-level notification settings (plus per-app Focus and Scheduled Summary allowances); there is no OS surface where a user tunes 'Low Glucose Alerts' separately from 'AI Notifications'. Notification categories and thread identifiers group and act on notifications but are not user-configurable.
impossible.closest_alternative: Move category granularity into the app: in-app per-category preferences (sound, whether the category is delivered at all) that the app honors when it builds each `UNNotificationRequest`. The upside is that the entire versioned-channel recreation mechanism, its lock, and its non-atomic increment hazard vanish, because on iOS sound and interruption level are per-request properties. The downside is that a user who mutes the app in iOS Settings mutes everything at once, which is exactly why the notification status card must report each suppressing condition.

impossible.capability: Raising the device's system alarm/ringer volume so a low-glucose alarm is loud regardless of how the phone is set ("Boost Volume for Lows" as implemented)
impossible.why: No iOS API sets system output volume, and none overrides the silent switch for ordinary notifications. `MPVolumeView` manipulation of system volume is unsupported for this purpose and would be rejected.
impossible.closest_alternative: Critical alerts: with the `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts` entitlement (Apple grants it only on request, typically to health and safety apps) and the user's `.criticalAlert` authorization, a notification with `.critical` interruption level and `UNNotificationSound.criticalSoundNamed(_:withAudioVolume:)` plays at an app-specified volume up to 1.0 and ignores both the silent switch and Focus. That delivers the user-facing outcome — a low alarm that is loud and unmissable — but it is an app-specified playback volume, not a change to the device's volume, and it is contingent on Apple approving the entitlement. Without the entitlement, the honest fallback is `.timeSensitive` (Focus bypass only, when the user permits) with copy that says plainly that the silent switch and volume can silence the alarm.

impossible.capability: An App Transport Security exception scoped to private/LAN IP ranges — allowing cleartext http:// to 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x and CGNAT while keeping ATS enforced for every public host
impossible.why: ATS exceptions are declared per-domain in Info.plist and do not accept IP addresses or CIDR ranges. `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` covers only unqualified single-label hostnames, `.local` names, and the link-local ranges (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10) — it does not cover RFC1918 addresses, which is the common self-hosting case. Worse, on modern iOS the presence of `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` causes `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads` to be ignored, so the two cannot be combined to get 'LAN cleartext plus ATS everywhere else'.
impossible.closest_alternative: Set `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = YES` with no `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` key and keep `UrlSecurityPolicy` as the in-app enforcement point — the exact architecture Android already uses, where the platform permits cleartext globally and the app is the sole guard preventing a public host from being reached over plaintext. This preserves the security property but moves it entirely into app code, requires an App Review justification for the blanket ATS exception, and means a policy bug is now the only thing between a user and cleartext to a public host. The alternative is to require https on iOS and point self-hosters at a reverse proxy, a trusted self-signed certificate, or a mesh VPN.

impossible.capability: A guaranteed long-running background execution window on demand (Android's foreground service holding the process for a 90-second LLM call, with an ongoing user-visible notification)
impossible.why: iOS has no foreground service. `beginBackgroundTask` grants roughly 30 seconds, is not guaranteed, and cannot be renewed; `BGTaskScheduler` runs opportunistically at times the system chooses and is unsuitable for on-demand work; and there is no mechanism to display an ongoing 'working…' notification tied to background execution.
impossible.closest_alternative: A background `URLSessionConfiguration` upload/download task, which the system runs out of process and delivers to the app via `handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession` even if the app was suspended or terminated — this achieves the outcome (the request completes and the answer arrives) but asynchronously, so any state the answer needs to land in must be persisted rather than held in memory. For the watch relay specifically, the better answer is to remove the need entirely by having the independent watchOS app call the backend directly, since watchOS routes its own `URLSession` over LTE, Wi-Fi, or the paired phone.

ios_requirements: The AI Chat tab must be present only when a server base URL is configured; when the app is in backend-optional local mode the tab must be absent and any deep link, restored navigation state, or widget tap targeting chat must return the user to Home without showing a blank screen.

On opening AI Chat the app must probe the server's AI provider exactly once and land in one of three terminal states: Ready, "No AI Provider Configured" (reached only from an HTTP 404, with the guidance to configure a provider in the web app and no action button), or "Unable to Connect" (reached from any other status or transport failure, with a Retry control). The app must not poll, retry automatically, or re-probe after a successful send; a spinner must never be a terminal state.

A user must be able to send a chat message of up to 2000 characters inclusive; a longer message must be refused locally with "Message is too long (max 2000 characters)" and no network request. The send control and the input field must be disabled while a request is in flight so a double-send is impossible.

The chat transcript must live only in memory, capped at the most recent 100 messages, and must be lost on process death — no chat content is persisted to disk. A Clear control must appear only when the transcript is non-empty and must clear the transcript, clear any error, and stop any speech in progress.

Chat failures must always present curated copy and never a raw error message: request timeout, no connectivity, session expired, server error, and an unclassified fallback each have their own fixed wording, rendered as a dismissible inline row at the bottom of the message list rather than a modal.

The chat screen must show four tappable starter suggestions when the transcript is empty; tapping one must only populate the input field, never send. A permanent footer above the input must read "AI responses are informational only. Always consult your healthcare provider." and each assistant reply must render the server-supplied disclaimer beneath it.

Assistant markdown must be sanitized before rendering: all image markdown and HTML image tags are stripped so AI-generated content can never trigger an outbound network fetch, and only http and https links may be opened — every other scheme is silently ignored.

A user must be able to turn spoken responses on and off from the chat screen, and while on, choose from the device's available speech voices for their language. Selecting a voice must persist it, survive relaunch, fall back to the system voice if the saved voice is no longer installed, and sync to the watch. Spoken output must always be the assistant's reply with ". This is not medical advice." appended, with markdown removed for natural reading; blank stripped text must not be spoken.
Speech must duck other audio rather than interrupt it, and must stop when the user turns speech off, clears the chat, or leaves the screen.
If a chat request is interrupted because the app left the foreground, the app must say so honestly on return and invite the user to resend, rather than leaving a stalled request indicator.

A user wearing the watch must be able to ask the AI a question from the watch and receive an answer on the watch, whether or not the phone app is open. Watch questions are limited to 500 characters, and the watch shows one question and one answer at a time with no transcript.

When no server is configured, a watch chat attempt must return the terminal message "AI chat needs a GlycemicGPT server — none is set up on your phone." and must not offer a retry, because retrying cannot succeed.

The watch must offer system dictation, scribble, and keyboard input for a question, plus three one-tap quick questions, and must speak the answer aloud when spoken responses are enabled — always with ". This is not medical advice." appended.
A user must be able to place a chat complication on their watch face and a chat widget in the Smart Stack; tapping either must open the watch chat screen, optionally pre-filled.

The watch must show a specific, honest failure for each condition — phone not connected, request timed out, no server configured, session expired — never a generic "something went wrong" when a more accurate cause is known. The watch's own timeout must not be shorter than the request timeout it is waiting on.

The app must not include an AI daily-brief screen. AI insights and briefs arrive only as server-pushed notifications, delivered in their own category at normal (non-critical, non-time-sensitive) priority, with their own configurable sound including an explicit Silent option.

Meal logging must be reachable only when a server is configured and meal intelligence is enabled; when the local setting is off the meal screen must show its disabled state immediately with no network request, and the server probe remains the authority. If the server reports the feature is off during an upload, the screen must move to its disabled state.

A user must be able to log a meal by taking a photo or choosing one from their library. Choosing from the library must not require a photo-library permission, and the chosen image must not carry location data. If camera access is denied the app must say so inline in error styling, keep the library path available, and offer a link to Settings, because iOS will not re-prompt.

Photos must be downscaled to a longest edge of 1280 pixels, oriented upright, and re-encoded as JPEG under 5 MiB by stepping quality down from 90 to 40 in steps of 10, failing with "Image is too large to upload after compression" if it still exceeds the cap. The uploaded bytes must contain no EXIF, GPS, or other metadata, and this must be verified by an automated test.

Temporary capture files must be deleted after upload, on cancellation, and when a new capture supersedes an old one; a full sweep runs only when the meal screen resets. A capture that is currently being read must never be deleted by another capture's cleanup.

The "Estimating carbs…" indicator must be impossible to leave stuck: every failure path clears it, image decoding must avoid loading a full-resolution bitmap so the app is not terminated for memory, oversized source images must be refused up front with "That photo is too large to process. Try a smaller one.", and if the app is terminated mid-upload the next launch must show an honest failure rather than resume into a spinner.

Every surface that displays a carb estimate must display, at the same time, "Rough estimate — an AI guess that's often wrong. Never use it to calculate an insulin dose or bolus." This applies to the meal result (pinned above the scroll region so it cannot scroll away), the meal history list, the common foods list, the re-log sheet, the edit sheet, and the Home recent-meal card. The qualifier must use a calm amber treatment, never the error/alarm color.

Carbs must always be presented as a low-to-high range with a confidence signal, never as a bare number; a single-point estimate still renders with units. Nothing in the meal feature may present insulin, units, or a bolus.
VoiceOver must announce the carb value, the confidence, the never-dose qualifier, and any uncertainty note as a single element, so the number can never be heard without the qualifier.
Confidence must be conveyed by bar length as well as color, and the medium and low levels must remain distinguishable without color perception.

When the estimate came from multiple reads that disagreed, or the AI was unsure what the food was, the app must show the server's uncertainty note in the caution treatment; when the reads agreed it must still show the note quietly, never implying the estimate is safe to dose from. Uncertainty information is available only on a newly created record and must never be fabricated for a history row.

A user must be able to confirm or correct what the food is, as an action separate from correcting the carbs, and the app must explain that confirming lets the estimate be grounded against real nutrition data. When the AI was unsure of the identity, the prompt must say so in error styling. A confirmed record must show that it was confirmed and allow the user to change it.

A user must be able to correct the carb range. Values must be rejected — never silently clamped — when either is not a number, is negative, exceeds 1000 grams, or when the low exceeds the high, each with its own message, and no invalid value may reach the server. The same validation and copy must be shared with the common-food editor. A corrected record must still show the original AI estimate alongside the correction.

A user must be able to ask "How was this estimated?" and see how many times the photo was read, what each read returned, and whether the result was grounded against an external source or is vision-only. This must load on demand only, and must be discarded when the food identity changes, because grounding and precedence have changed.

When the server returns nutrition information the app must render it verbatim in the server's own words — the assumed portion with its prompt to check portion size, macros in whole units with their glucose notes, net carbs behind their caveat and clearly secondary to the total range, and the section disclaimer. Any non-finite or malformed number must be dropped rather than displayed, and a block with nothing left to show must not render at all.

Heart and blood-pressure nutrition information must appear only for a confirmed, grounded record, attributed to its source and trust tier, and must be framed as awareness rather than a directive. A sugar caveat must not appear if the sugar value it refers to was dropped.
A user must be able to save a meal's estimate as a named common food, see it confirmed by the name the server returned, and be told when that name is already taken.

When the server is unreachable, meal history and common foods must show a clear "can't reach your server" state with a Retry control — never an empty-list message that would imply the user has logged nothing. When a list is already loaded and a refresh fails, the failure must appear as a small inline notice above the existing list rather than replacing it.

A user must be able to delete a meal record or a common food with immediate effect and no confirmation, with any failure surfaced as a transient message; pump unpairing and driver deactivation must keep their confirmations.

A user must be able to re-log a saved common food by viewing its saved carb range in a read-only sheet that carries the never-dose qualifier — this must not create a new record, matching the current server capability.

Home must show the most recent meal with its carb range, confidence, timestamp, and the never-dose qualifier, and must offer a single obvious entry point to log a meal. The meal entry point must be absent when no server is configured or meal intelligence is off, and must remain available when a probe fails for transient reasons so the meal screen can present its own degraded state.

First-run onboarding must present welcome, features, a safety disclaimer, optional server setup, and sign-in, and the safety disclaimer must be impossible to skip or swipe past — only an explicit "I Understand" advances it. The disclaimer must include a card stating that photo carb estimates are AI guesses that are frequently wrong, can misidentify the food entirely, and must never be used to calculate an insulin dose or bolus.

A user must be able to finish onboarding without a server and use the app as a direct pump monitor; taking that path must cancel any in-flight connection test before clearing the saved server URL, and must clear any server-supplied alert thresholds so a departed server's values are never left armed.

Both onboarding completion paths — after sign-in and after choosing local-only mode — must request notification permission before navigating away, and that single request must include the critical-alert option, because iOS grants the prompt only once and the on-device alert floor is silently suppressed without permission.

A user must be able to test their server connection before signing in, see a clear success or failure result, and have the typed URL restored to the previous working value if the test fails. Repeated taps within one second must be ignored.

If iOS blocks access to a server on the local network, the app must say exactly that and link the user to the Local Network setting, rather than reporting a generic connection failure. This must be distinguishable in the UI from a wrong URL, a down server, and an insecure-scheme rejection.

A user must be able to opt in to reaching a self-hosted server over unencrypted http on a private or LAN address, only after acknowledging a dialog that states the traffic is unencrypted and readable by anyone on the network, and only for private/LAN addresses — public addresses must always require https. The opt-in must be available inline during onboarding, because a new user cannot reach Settings before signing in.

While insecure LAN http is actually in use, a persistent banner must appear above every screen including onboarding, and it must appear only when cleartext would genuinely be sent — never for a public http URL the app refuses to contact.

Host classification for the LAN exception must never perform a DNS lookup, must accept only strictly-formatted IP literals (rejecting octal, hexadecimal, bare-decimal, and leading-zero forms) plus mDNS names ending in .local with at least one label, and must classify IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses by their embedded IPv4.

Sign-in credentials, the access token, its expiry, and the refresh token must be stored in the system keychain and must remain readable while the device is locked after the first unlock, so overnight token refresh and background alert handling cannot fail silently. The password must be cleared from app state on both success and failure.

The app must choose its start destination from whether onboarding was completed, independent of whether the session is still valid, so an expired session can never re-onboard a user or lock locally-cached pump data behind an impossible sign-in.

Settings must present Account, Network, Drivers, Sync, Meal Intelligence, Notifications, Watch, Appearance, About, and (debug builds only) Developer, in that order, and must refresh its state every time the screen is shown.

In backend-optional local mode, Settings must hide the backend sync control, the meal intelligence section, and the AI notification sound row while keeping data retention, low and high alert sounds, and everything else — and must switch the alert-threshold editor from read-only to editable.

Alert thresholds must be read-only whenever a server is configured, showing the four current values, the unit, and a note that they are managed on the server, or "Waiting for the first sync from your server." when none has arrived. Saving a server URL must make the editor read-only in the same interaction, and any save attempt must re-check the live backend state before writing.

In local-only mode a user must be able to set all four thresholds in their chosen unit. All four must land within 20–500 mg/dL and satisfy urgent low ≤ low < high ≤ urgent high, values are stored canonically in mg/dL, and out-of-range or out-of-order input is rejected with a specific message — never clamped. The mmol/L bounds quoted in the error message must themselves be values that round back into the accepted mg/dL range.

On-device alarms must not fire from default thresholds. Until thresholds arrive from a server or are saved locally, Settings must state in error styling that on-device alarms are off until all four are set.
Alert thresholds must be written durably before the save is reported as complete, and must remain readable by the alerting path while the device is locked.
Signing out must clear server-supplied alert thresholds so the alarm floor cannot fire from a departed account's values, while preserving thresholds the user set on this device.

A user must be able to choose a sound for low alerts, high alerts, and AI notifications from a set of sounds included in the app, preview each one, and choose Silent for AI notifications. Low-alert sounds must be distinctly alarm-like.

Low and high glucose alerts must attempt to break through Focus and Do Not Disturb, and low alerts must be able to sound at full volume even when the device is silenced, using critical alerts where the entitlement is available. Low alerts must re-alert on each update; high and AI alerts alert once. If critical alerts are unavailable, the app must say plainly that the phone's silent switch and volume can silence the alarm rather than implying protection it does not have.

The notification status card must report every condition that would prevent an alert reaching the user — permission denied, sound off, critical alerts not permitted, Time Sensitive not permitted, Scheduled Summary enabled — each with a link to the relevant setting, and must re-check every time the app returns to the foreground.

Settings must show whether the watch is paired, whether the watch app is installed, and whether it is currently reachable, plus the last glucose and insulin-on-board values sent to the watch with their age, labelled explicitly as canonical wire values in mg/dL. Values outside 20–500 mg/dL must be shown as unavailable.

A user must be able to configure what the watch app and its complications show — insulin on board, the glucose graph and its 1/3/6-hour range, alert vibration, theme, and the graph overlays — with changes taking effect on the watch without further action.

Because watchOS does not support third-party watch faces, the app must deliver glanceable data through watch complications the user places on an Apple face and through Smart Stack widgets, and must explain in Settings how to add them. Settings must not offer a watch-face gallery or a face push.
Settings must show the installed phone and watch app versions, flag a mismatch, and direct the user to TestFlight to update; the app must not attempt to download or install any build itself.
A user must be able to choose System, Dark, or Light appearance, per device, and the choice must apply immediately across the app, including to the calm-caution treatment used by safety notes.

A user must be able to display glucose in mg/dL or mmol/L. All storage, transport, thresholds, alert evaluation, watch payloads, and the 20–500 safety range remain mg/dL; the choice affects display and speech only. Conversion uses a single constant of 18.0156, converts once from the most precise source, and rounds last; a spread or standard deviation converts without the offset.
When the app has picked a unit automatically from region or a data source, it must say so once above the selector with a dismissible note, and must never block the UI with it.

A user must be able to enable or disable meal intelligence for their account, with the local effect immediate and the account sync attempted afterwards. When the sync fails the app must say "Saved on this device. Couldn't sync to your account." and must not imply it will retry. Rapid toggling must never let a stale response overwrite a newer choice, and a rejected account must fail closed to disabled.
A user must be able to set local data retention between 1 and 30 days, defaulting to 7, and that value must bound the analysis windows offered elsewhere.

A user must be able to open the app's open-source license documents with no connectivity, select and copy text across paragraph boundaries, and return to their previous scroll position after a rotation or size change. The screen must state nothing of its own about licensing — every word comes from a document generated from the repository at build time, and a build whose license documents are missing or empty must fail rather than ship.

Debug builds only must expose a developer section with a driver debug console, a pump-label toggle, a simulate-backend-unreachable fault, and a compressed-staleness fault; these must be compiled out of release builds entirely, and the fault toggles must additionally refuse to act in a release build.

The debug console must let a developer inject a normal glucose reading, a fresh low reading, and a stale low reading through the same code path a real reading takes, so the alert floor's fire and suppress behaviors and the honest "NOT watching" surface can be validated without pump hardware — which is the only way to exercise them in the Simulator.

When the session has expired, or when a server is configured but the user is not signed in, a tappable banner must appear that takes the user to Settings; a user in local-only mode must never see it, because being signed out is that mode's normal state.

risks.risk: The Critical Alerts entitlement (`com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts`) is granted only by Apple on written request and is not guaranteed for an unofficial, non-FDA-cleared diabetes app. Without it, a low-glucose alarm cannot bypass the silent switch or a muted volume — the single most safety-relevant behavior in the whole app degrades to something the phone can silence.
risks.mitigation: Apply for the entitlement at the very start of the project, before any UI is built, citing the low-glucose alarm and the existing safety architecture (validated thresholds, the never-fires-from-defaults rule, the honest degradation surfaces). Design the alert layer so interruption level and sound are a single injectable policy, so the fallback to Time Sensitive is a configuration change, not a rewrite. Ship the fallback copy that plainly states the phone can silence the alarm, and make the notification status card report `criticalAlertSetting` so the user always knows which regime they are in. Note that provisioning profiles are not enforced in the Simulator, so an ungranted entitlement will appear to work there — validate on device.

risks.risk: Reaching a self-hosted server on an RFC1918 address over http requires `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`, a blanket ATS exemption that must be justified at review (TestFlight's first build goes through Beta App Review). A rejection or a demand to remove it would break the LAN self-hosting story that the insecure-LAN-HTTP opt-in exists to serve.
risks.mitigation: Decide the ATS posture before writing the networking layer (see the PM question). If the blanket exemption is taken, keep `UrlSecurityPolicy` as a hard, exhaustively unit-tested guard and be prepared to explain at review that the app enforces private-address-only cleartext in code because ATS cannot express CIDR ranges. Keep the acknowledgement dialog and the persistent insecure-mode banner — they are exactly the kind of user-informed-consent evidence review responds well to. Have the https-only fallback designed so it can ship without a redesign.

risks.risk: iOS 14+ Local Network Privacy will block connections to a LAN server until the user grants permission, the prompt appears only once, denial is not re-promptable in-app, and — critically — the Simulator does not present or enforce this prompt. The developer's entire Simulator loop will show a working LAN connection while every real device fails with an opaque error.
risks.mitigation: Declare `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` from day one, drive the permission deliberately during the onboarding connection test, and build a specific, distinguishable UI state for denial with a Settings deep link. Add a device-based smoke test for the LAN path to the definition of done for onboarding and Settings, and write the trap into the project's testing notes so it is not rediscovered late.

risks.risk: Keychain accessibility classes and file data-protection classes are not enforced in the Simulator. Storing the refresh token or the alert thresholds with a when-unlocked protection class will pass every Simulator test and then fail silently on a real, locked phone overnight — exactly when the alert floor matters most.
risks.mitigation: Standardize on `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` for the token and `.completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication` for the threshold and settings stores, enforce it in a single storage wrapper rather than at call sites, and add a device-only test that reads both while the screen is locked. Treat 'works in Simulator' as no evidence at all for anything lock-state dependent.

risks.risk: App Review and Beta App Review scrutiny of a medical-adjacent app that displays AI-generated carb estimates. Guideline 1.4.1 covers apps that could cause physical harm, and an AI estimate adjacent to insulin dosing is precisely the pattern reviewers probe.
risks.mitigation: The existing safety architecture is the mitigation and must not be diluted in the port: the never-dose qualifier on every estimate surface, the un-skippable onboarding disclaimer card that names the prohibited action, the range-plus-confidence presentation that never yields a bare number, the merged VoiceOver phrase, and the app-wide monitoring-only, no-therapeutic-writes posture. Put these in the reviewer notes explicitly. Also disclose the read-only nature of pump interaction, since 'diabetes app' plus 'pump' will otherwise read as a dosing app.

risks.risk: Losing custom watch faces is the most visible regression for existing Android users, and no combination of complications, Smart Stack widgets, and shareable Apple faces reproduces the Digital Full / Analog Mechanical designs with their basal, bolus, IoB, and activity-mode graph overlays.
risks.mitigation: State the gap plainly in the PRD rather than describing the substitutes as parity. Invest the recovered effort in the watch app's own main screen (which can render the full graph with all four overlays exactly as designed) and in an `accessoryRectangular` complication that carries the graph onto whatever face the user chooses. Consider bundled `.watchface` files as a low-cost way to give users a one-tap curated starting point.

risks.risk: The 90-second AI request does not survive iOS app suspension, so a behavior Android users have — ask a question, switch apps, come back to the answer — silently disappears, and the in-memory-only transcript means a background-delivered answer has nowhere to land.
risks.mitigation: Make the narrower contract explicit and visible: cancel on background and tell the user on return. Reserve background URLSession delivery for the watch-relay fallback path, where the user is not watching the phone. Do not add chat persistence just to preserve this — it would create a durable store of health-related conversation content that the Android app deliberately does not have.

risks.risk: The iOS Simulator has no camera, so the meal capture path — the primary entry point for the entire meal subsystem — cannot be exercised in the developer's main loop. The library path can, but only against the seeded photo library.
risks.mitigation: Extend the existing debug-injection philosophy: add a debug-only 'use a bundled sample meal photo' action beside the camera button that feeds the same compression and upload path, including deliberately oversized and unusually-oriented samples so the downscale, orientation, quality ladder, and metadata-stripping behaviors are all exercisable in the Simulator. Reserve real-camera validation for device passes.

risks.risk: watchOS dictation does not function in the watchOS Simulator, so the watch chat's primary input mechanism cannot be validated in the developer's loop; text falls through to the Mac keyboard, which hides the truncation, blank-input, and cancellation behaviors.
risks.mitigation: Keep the three quick-query buttons and the widget-deep-link prefill as fully Simulator-testable paths covering the same downstream state machine, and unit-test truncation and blank handling on the plain string input. Schedule a device pass specifically for watch input before any release.

risks.risk: Notification behavior is only partially observable in the Simulator: local notifications do fire and remote payloads can be delivered with `xcrun simctl push`, but the Simulator has no ring/silent switch and does not enforce Focus, so critical-alert bypass, sound routing, and volume simply cannot be validated there.
risks.mitigation: Treat every alert-delivery acceptance criterion as device-only. Add a debug action that posts each alert category with its real content, sound, and interruption level so a device pass is one tap rather than a reproduction exercise, and pair it with the existing fresh-low and stale-low injections so the fire-versus-suppress safety pair is testable end to end.

risks.risk: Persisted TTS voice identifiers, watch-face variant names, and FAB offsets from Android have no meaning on iOS, and the alert-sound URIs cannot be migrated at all. Any assumption of settings continuity for a user moving platforms is false.
risks.mitigation: There is no cross-platform settings migration path, so do not build one. Ensure every setting has a safe default and that an unresolvable persisted value falls back cleanly (unknown voice → system voice; unknown sound → category default), which the Android code already does for voices and face variants.

risks.risk: The license-attribution build step must be reimplemented against SwiftPM, which has no equivalent of Gradle's resolved release runtime dependency graph. A weaker implementation would break the invariant that a dependency cannot enter the build without entering the attribution.
risks.mitigation: Drive the generator from `Package.resolved` plus an explicit manifest of any vendored or binary dependencies, fail the build when a resolved package has no matching license entry, and keep the existing rules that a missing README License section or an empty source document fails the build rather than shipping a blank section.

questions_for_pm: Which ATS posture should iOS take for self-hosted servers: (a) set `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads` and keep the existing in-app private-address-only policy as the sole guard — preserving parity with Android's insecure-LAN-HTTP opt-in but requiring a blanket cleartext exemption to be justified at Beta App Review and every subsequent review, or (b) require https on iOS, drop the insecure-LAN-HTTP opt-in entirely, and direct self-hosters to a reverse proxy, a trusted certificate, or a mesh VPN? Apple permits both, the Android repo cannot answer it, and it is a genuine tradeoff between reaching plain-http LAN self-hosters and carrying a standing review risk on a safety-critical app.
